blocks.body:
A turnstile, a vending machine and the part of a compiler that splits code into words all do the same thing: they read input symbols one at a time and react according to a current state, of which there are only finitely many. A finite automaton is the mathematical model of such a device.

The model is simple enough that one can answer, with proof, exactly which tasks it can do. Can a machine with finite memory check whether a binary number is divisible by 3? Yes, with three states. Can it check whether a string of brackets is balanced? No, and the reason (it would have to count arbitrarily high) is made precise by the pumping lemma. Along the way, different-looking models turn out to have exactly the same power.

blocks.title: Strings and languages
blocks.body:
An alphabet $\Sigma$ is a finite nonempty set of symbols, for example $\{0, 1\}$ or $\{a, b\}$. A string (or word) over $\Sigma$ is a finite sequence of symbols; its length is written $|w|$, and the empty string, of length 0, is $\varepsilon$. The set of all strings is $\Sigma^*$. A language is any subset $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ (see [[sets-relations]]).

Strings are joined by concatenation: if $x = 01$ and $y = 110$ then $xy = 01110$. For languages, $AB = \{xy : x \in A, y \in B\}$, and the star $A^* = \{\varepsilon\} \cup A \cup AA \cup AAA \cup \cdots$ is the set of all concatenations of finitely many strings from $A$. Write $y^i$ for $y$ repeated $i$ times, with $y^0 = \varepsilon$.

Examples of languages over $\{0,1\}$: all strings ending in 1; binary representations of multiples of 3; strings with no two consecutive 1s; $\{0^n 1^n : n \ge 0\}$. The question is which of these a finite machine can recognise.

blocks.title: Deterministic finite automaton
blocks.body:
A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a 5-tuple $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ where $Q$ is a finite set of states, $\Sigma$ an alphabet, $\delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q$ the transition function, $q_0 \in Q$ the start state and $F \subseteq Q$ the set of accepting states.

Extend $\delta$ to strings recursively: $\delta^*(q, \varepsilon) = q$ and $\delta^*(q, wa) = \delta(\delta^*(q, w), a)$ for a string $w$ and symbol $a$. The language of $M$ is

$$L(M) = \{ w \in \Sigma^* : \delta^*(q_0, w) \in F \}.$$

A language is regular if some DFA recognises it. In words: start in $q_0$, follow one arrow per symbol, and accept if you finish in an accepting state.

blocks.title: Designing automata: remember only what matters
blocks.body:
The design question is always: what is the least information about the part of the string read so far that lets me finish the job? The states are exactly that information.

Multiples of 3 in binary. Reading a binary number from the left, if the part read so far has value $v$, appending a digit $a$ gives value $2v + a$. So whether the final number is divisible by 3 depends only on $v \bmod 3$, and that can be updated: the new remainder is $(2r + a) \bmod 3$. Take $Q = \{0, 1, 2\}$, $q_0 = 0$, $F = \{0\}$ and $\delta(r, a) = (2r + a) \bmod 3$. A proof that it works is an induction on the length of the input (see [[induction]]): $\delta^*(0, w)$ equals the value of $w$ modulo 3. The same idea gives an $m$-state DFA for multiples of any $m$, using [[congruences]].

No two consecutive 1s. Remember whether the last symbol was a 1, and whether a forbidden pair has already appeared: states "last was 0 or start" (A), "last was 1" (B) and "dead" (D). Transitions: from A, 0 goes to A and 1 to B; from B, 0 goes to A and 1 to D; D goes to D on both. Accepting states $\{A, B\}$.

Finite-state machines with output, such as a vending machine that emits a product or change, are the same idea with an output symbol attached to each transition (a Mealy machine) or to each state (a Moore machine). Recognising languages is the special case where the only output is accept or reject at the end.

blocks.title: Nondeterministic finite automaton
blocks.body:
A nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) is like a DFA except that the transition function is $\delta : Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \to \mathcal{P}(Q)$: from a state, a symbol may lead to several states or none, and $\varepsilon$-moves change state without reading anything. An NFA accepts $w$ if at least one way of following the arrows while reading all of $w$ ends in an accepting state.

In words: the machine may guess, and it accepts if some lucky sequence of guesses works.

blocks.title: Subset construction
blocks.body: For every NFA $N$ with state set $Q$ there is a DFA $D$ with at most $2^{|Q|}$ states such that $L(D) = L(N)$. Hence NFAs recognise exactly the regular languages.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
For a set $S$ of states let $E(S)$ be the set of states reachable from $S$ by $\varepsilon$-moves alone (including $S$ itself). The states of $D$ are subsets of $Q$. Its start state is $E(\{q_0\})$, its transition is

$$\Delta(S, a) = E\Big(\bigcup_{q \in S} \delta(q, a)\Big),$$

and $S$ is accepting if $S$ contains an accepting state of $N$. By induction on $|w|$, $\Delta^*(E(\{q_0\}), w)$ is exactly the set of states $N$ can be in after reading $w$: true for $w = \varepsilon$ by definition, and the formula for $\Delta$ is precisely one step of "all possible moves". So $D$ accepts $w$ if and only if some run of $N$ on $w$ ends in an accepting state.

blocks.title: Regular expressions and Kleene's theorem
blocks.body:
Regular expressions build languages from single symbols using three operations: union ($R \mid S$), concatenation ($RS$) and star ($R^*$), together with $\varepsilon$ and the empty language $\emptyset$. For instance $(0 \mid 1)^*1$ describes strings ending in 1, and $(0 \mid 10)^*(\varepsilon \mid 1)$ describes strings with no two consecutive 1s: break the string after each 0, and every piece is 0 or 10, except possibly a final 1.

Kleene's theorem: a language is regular if and only if it is described by a regular expression. Proof sketch. From expression to automaton: build NFAs by induction on the expression; for a union, add a new start state with $\varepsilon$-moves to the two machines; for a concatenation, add $\varepsilon$-moves from the accepting states of the first to the start of the second; for a star, add a new accepting start state with an $\varepsilon$-move to the old start, and $\varepsilon$-moves from the old accepting states back to the old start. Then apply the subset construction. From automaton to expression: remove states one at a time, labelling arrows by regular expressions for the paths they replace, until only a start and an accepting state remain.

Closure properties follow cheaply. The complement of a regular language is regular: swap accepting and non-accepting states of a DFA. The intersection of two regular languages is regular: run both DFAs at once on pairs of states $(p, q)$, accepting when both components accept (the product construction). Union, concatenation and star come from Kleene's theorem.

blocks.title: Pumping lemma for regular languages
blocks.body:
If $L$ is regular, there is an integer $p \ge 1$ (a pumping length) such that every $w \in L$ with $|w| \ge p$ can be written $w = xyz$ with

1. $|xy| \le p$,
2. $|y| \ge 1$,
3. $xy^iz \in L$ for every $i \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: Let $M$ be a DFA for $L$ with $p$ states. Read $w = a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ with $n \ge p$ and list the states visited after $0, 1, \dots, p$ symbols: $s_0 = q_0, s_1, \dots, s_p$. These are $p + 1$ states from a set of size $p$, so by the [[pigeonhole]] principle $s_j = s_k$ for some $0 \le j < k \le p$. Let $x = a_1 \cdots a_j$, $y = a_{j+1} \cdots a_k$ and $z$ the rest. Then $|xy| = k \le p$ and $|y| = k - j \ge 1$. Reading $y$ takes the machine from $s_j$ back to the same state, so the loop can be traversed any number of times, including zero: $\delta^*(q_0, xy^iz) = \delta^*(q_0, xyz) \in F$ for every $i \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Tracing a run
blocks.body: Run the multiples-of-3 automaton on $w = 1101$ and on $w = 10010$. What do the results mean?
blocks.solution:
On $1101$: start in 0; reading 1 gives $(0 + 1) \bmod 3 = 1$; reading 1 gives $(2 + 1) \bmod 3 = 0$; reading 0 gives 0; reading 1 gives 1. The final state 1 is not accepting, so the string is rejected. Indeed $1101_2 = 13 = 3 \cdot 4 + 1$.

On $10010$: from 0, reading 1 gives 1; reading 0 gives $2 \bmod 3 = 2$; reading 0 gives $4 \bmod 3 = 1$; reading 1 gives $3 \bmod 3 = 0$; reading 0 gives 0. The run $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 1 \to 0 \to 0$ ends in an accepting state, and indeed $10010_2 = 18 = 3 \cdot 6$. Tracing by hand is error-prone; the invariant "state = value of the prefix mod 3" is the reliable check.

blocks.title: From guessing to determinism
blocks.body: Let $L$ be the set of strings over $\{0,1\}$ whose second-to-last symbol is 1. Give a 3-state NFA for $L$, convert it to a DFA, and show that every DFA for $L$ needs at least 4 states.
blocks.solution:
NFA: state $a$ loops on 0 and 1; on reading 1 it may also guess "this is the second-to-last symbol" and move to $b$; from $b$ any symbol leads to $c$, which is accepting and has no outgoing arrows.

Subset construction from $\{a\}$: on 0 stay at $\{a\}$, on 1 go to $\{a, b\}$. From $\{a,b\}$: 0 gives $\{a, c\}$, 1 gives $\{a, b, c\}$. From $\{a, c\}$: 0 gives $\{a\}$, 1 gives $\{a, b\}$. From $\{a, b, c\}$: 0 gives $\{a, c\}$, 1 gives $\{a, b, c\}$. Four reachable subsets; the accepting ones are those containing $c$. In effect the DFA remembers the last two symbols read, counting missing symbols at the start as 0: $\{a\}$ means "00", $\{a,b\}$ means "01", $\{a,c\}$ means "10" and $\{a,b,c\}$ means "11".

Lower bound: take the four strings $00, 01, 10, 11$. For any two of them there is a suffix $z$ that sends one into $L$ and the other out. For example $10$ and $00$ differ on $z = \varepsilon$; $01$ and $00$ differ on $z = 0$ (giving $010 \in L$, $000 \notin L$); in general if two two-symbol strings differ in the first position use $z = \varepsilon$, and if they differ only in the second use $z = 0$. A DFA that sent two of them to the same state would treat them identically for every suffix. So the four strings reach four different states.

The same argument shows that "the $k$-th symbol from the end is 1" has a $(k+1)$-state NFA but needs $2^k$ states as a DFA: the exponential blow-up in the subset construction can really happen.

blocks.title: Not regular
blocks.body: Show that $L = \{0^n 1^n : n \ge 0\}$ is not regular. Deduce that the language of balanced bracket strings is not regular.
blocks.solution:
Suppose $L$ is regular with pumping length $p$. Take $w = 0^p 1^p \in L$. In any decomposition $w = xyz$ with $|xy| \le p$ and $|y| \ge 1$, the part $y$ lies inside the first $p$ symbols, so $y = 0^m$ with $m \ge 1$. Then $xy^2z = 0^{p+m}1^p$ has more 0s than 1s and is not in $L$, contradicting the lemma.

For brackets, write 0 for "(" and 1 for ")". If the balanced strings $B$ formed a regular language, then so would $B \cap 0^*1^*$, by the product construction, since $0^*1^*$ is regular. But a balanced string of the form $0^a1^b$ must have $a = b$, so $B \cap 0^*1^* = L$, which is not regular.

The idea: a finite machine cannot count without bound. After reading $0^n$ for $n$ larger than the number of states, two different counts land in the same state, and from then on the machine cannot tell them apart.

blocks.title: Counting accepted strings
blocks.body: How many binary strings of length 10 contain no two consecutive 1s?
blocks.solution:
Use the 3-state automaton A, B, D above. Let $A_n$ and $B_n$ be the numbers of strings of length $n$ that end in states A and B (strings ending in D are rejected). A string ends in A if its last symbol is 0 and it was in A or B before; it ends in B if the last symbol is 1 and it was in A before. So

$$A_n = A_{n-1} + B_{n-1}, \qquad B_n = A_{n-1},$$

with $A_0 = 1$, $B_0 = 0$. The total $t_n = A_n + B_n$ satisfies $t_n = t_{n-1} + t_{n-2}$, with $t_0 = 1$ and $t_1 = 2$, so $t_n = F_{n+2}$ (Fibonacci numbers with $F_1 = F_2 = 1$). For $n = 10$: $t_{10} = F_{12} = 144$.

The method is general: for any DFA, the number of accepted strings of length $n$ is $u^{\mathsf{T}} P^n v$, where $P_{st}$ counts the symbols leading from state $s$ to state $t$, $u$ marks the start state and $v$ the accepting states, so it satisfies a linear recurrence and has a rational [[generating-functions|generating function]].

blocks.body:
- The pumping lemma only goes one way. Every regular language satisfies it, but some non-regular languages satisfy it too, so it can prove non-regularity, never regularity.
- In a pumping argument you choose $w$ but not the decomposition: the contradiction must hold for every split $xyz$ with $|xy| \le p$ and $|y| \ge 1$.
- Finite languages are always regular, and infinite languages may well be regular: $(0 \mid 1)^*$ is infinite and recognised by one state.
- Nondeterminism does not add power to finite automata, but the equivalent DFA can be exponentially larger.
- A DFA must have a transition for every state and symbol. Diagrams often omit a dead state; remember it is there.

Regular languages are the bottom level of the Chomsky hierarchy. Adding a stack gives pushdown automata, which recognise the context-free languages (balanced brackets, most programming-language syntax). Adding an unbounded read-write tape gives Turing machines, the subject of [[computability]], where some questions about machines become undecidable; for DFAs, by contrast, almost everything is decidable: emptiness, equality of two languages and minimisation can all be computed. Automata also appear in logic (Büchi's theorem links them to monadic second-order logic, see [[logic-basics]]), in combinatorics on words, and in [[algorithms]] for pattern matching such as the Knuth–Morris–Pratt method.

1. Design a DFA over $\{0, 1\}$ accepting exactly the strings with an even number of 0s and an odd number of 1s. How many states are needed?
2. Write a regular expression for the strings over $\{a, b\}$ that contain $ab$ as a substring, and build a 3-state DFA for the same language.
3. Use the pumping lemma to show that $\{0^{n^2} : n \ge 0\}$ is not regular.
4. Show that if $L$ is regular then so is its reversal $\{a_n \cdots a_1 : a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$.
